blocks.en: 1. A Man Walks Out of a Tomb
blocks.es_reference: 1. Un hombre sale de una tumba

blocks.en: Bethany is less than two miles from Jerusalem. Four days after Lazarus is buried, his sisters are still receiving mourners. The cave that holds the body is sealed with a stone. The smell of decay has begun. Then a Galilean rabbi walks up the road. He has been delayed on purpose — He could have come earlier and prevented the death. He stops at the cave. He weeps in front of the stone. He commands the stone to be moved. He raises His eyes to His Father. Then He says four words: Lazarus, come out. And the dead man walks out, his graveclothes still wrapped around him.
blocks.es_reference: Betania está a menos de tres kilómetros de Jerusalén. Cuatro días después de que Lázaro es enterrado, sus hermanas todavía reciben a los que vienen a llorar. La cueva que contiene el cuerpo está sellada con una piedra. El olor de la descomposición ha comenzado. Entonces un rabí galileo sube por el camino. Se ha demorado a propósito — podría haber venido antes y haber impedido la muerte. Se detiene en la cueva. Llora frente a la piedra. Manda que la piedra se quite. Levanta los ojos al Padre. Luego dice cuatro palabras: Lázaro, ven fuera. Y el muerto sale, con los lienzos sepulcrales todavía envueltos a su alrededor.

blocks.en: Read the chapter and you will see something the casual reader misses. Before Jesus walks to the tomb, He says one sentence that explains everything that is about to happen:
blocks.es_reference: Lea el capítulo y verá algo que el lector casual pierde. Antes de que Jesús vaya a la tumba, dice una sola oración que explica todo lo que está a punto de suceder:

blocks.en: “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in Me, though he may die, he shall live.” (John 11:25, NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: «Yo soy la resurrección y la vida; el que cree en mí, aunque esté muerto, vivirá.» (Juan 11:25, RVG)

blocks.en: Jesus speaks the sentence to Martha while Lazarus is still in the tomb. Minutes later He stands in front of the cave and performs what He has just declared. The words and the act are one teaching. The miracle is not separate from the sermon. The miracle is the sermon. That is the principle of this unit.
blocks.es_reference: Jesús pronuncia la oración a Marta mientras Lázaro está todavía en la tumba. Minutos después se para frente a la cueva y realiza lo que acaba de declarar. Las palabras y el acto son una sola enseñanza. El milagro no está separado del sermón. El milagro es el sermón. Ése es el principio de esta unidad.

blocks.en: 2. The Principle
blocks.es_reference: 2. El principio

blocks.en: Christ’s miracles are not random displays of power. They are not advertising for His ministry. They are not stunts to attract a crowd. Many of them also function as enacted signs — they preach as well as demonstrate power and compassion. The Greek word the Apostle John prefers for Jesus’ miracles is sêmeion — sign. A sign is something that points beyond itself. Where Scripture itself draws out that pointing, as John does again and again, the miracle is the visible word, and the spoken word interprets it.
blocks.es_reference: Los milagros de Cristo no son despliegues de poder al azar. No son publicidad para Su ministerio. No son trucos para atraer multitudes. Muchos de ellos también funcionan como señales representadas — predican tanto como demuestran poder y compasión. La palabra griega que el apóstol Juan prefiere para los milagros de Jesús es sêmeion — señal. Una señal es algo que apunta más allá de sí misma. Donde la Escritura misma extrae ese señalamiento, como hace Juan una y otra vez, el milagro es la palabra visible, y la palabra pronunciada la interpreta.

blocks.en: Treat a miracle as a spectacle and you will preach a thrill. Treat a miracle as an enacted parable and you will preach the gospel. The fish were not the point of the feeding of the five thousand. The bread was not the point. The point was the Bread of Life, which Jesus declared aloud the next day in John 6. The miracle preached. Then the spoken word interpreted the miracle.
blocks.es_reference: Trate un milagro como un espectáculo y predicará una emoción. Trate un milagro como una parábola representada y predicará el evangelio. Los peces no eran el punto de la alimentación de los cinco mil. El pan no era el punto. El punto era el Pan de Vida, que Jesús declaró en voz alta al día siguiente en Juan 6. El milagro predicó. Luego la palabra pronunciada interpretó el milagro.

blocks.en: 3. Lazarus as Enacted Parable
blocks.es_reference: 3. Lázaro como parábola representada

blocks.en: The raising of Lazarus has four movements, and each one is part of a single sermon Jesus is preaching with His hands and His voice together.
blocks.es_reference: La resurrección de Lázaro tiene cuatro movimientos, y cada uno es parte de un solo sermón que Jesús está predicando con Sus manos y Su voz juntas.

blocks.en: The tragedy of death. Lazarus dies, even though Jesus is told he is sick. Death is not gentle in the Bible. When my sister’s infant daughter died after a routine operation when I was fifteen, my first experience with death was the death of a child who had not yet learned to walk. Death is a tragedy when a young man dies. It is a tragedy when an unbeliever dies. It is a tragedy when a long illness finally takes someone. The Lord acknowledged the tragedy — Jesus wept, John tells us, in the shortest verse in the Bible. He did not pretend death was nothing. He wept at it.
blocks.es_reference: La tragedia de la muerte. Lázaro muere, aun cuando le dicen a Jesús que está enfermo. La muerte no es gentil en la Biblia. Cuando la hija pequeña de mi hermana murió después de una operación rutinaria cuando yo tenía quince años, mi primera experiencia con la muerte fue la muerte de una niña que aún no había aprendido a caminar. La muerte es una tragedia cuando un joven muere. Es una tragedia cuando un incrédulo muere. Es una tragedia cuando una larga enfermedad finalmente se lleva a alguien. El Señor reconoció la tragedia — Jesús lloró, nos dice Juan, en el versículo más corto de la Biblia. No fingió que la muerte no era nada. Lloró por ella.

blocks.en: The trial of death. Jesus could have come early. He stayed where He was two more days. The disciples did not understand. Martha did not understand. Mary did not understand. Jesus was teaching them — and us — that God’s timing is not our timing, and that delay is part of how He prepares His people to see His glory. The miracle would not have been a miracle if Jesus had arrived in time to prevent the death. The delay was the canvas on which the miracle would be painted.
blocks.es_reference: La prueba de la muerte. Jesús podría haber venido temprano. Se quedó donde estaba dos días más. Los discípulos no entendieron. Marta no entendió. María no entendió. Jesús les estaba enseñando — y nos está enseñando — que el tiempo de Dios no es nuestro tiempo, y que la demora es parte de cómo Él prepara a Su pueblo para ver Su gloria. El milagro no habría sido un milagro si Jesús hubiera llegado a tiempo para prevenir la muerte. La demora era el lienzo sobre el cual se pintaría el milagro.

blocks.en: The tears of death. Mary weeps. Martha weeps. The professional mourners weep. The Jewish neighbors weep. And Jesus weeps. Many years ago I sat with a woman whose husband had left her for another woman. She was holding back her grief, refusing to let it be real. The day she finally let herself cry was the day she began to heal. Tears are part of how God lets the heart loose. The Lord did not deny the tears at Bethany. He shed them Himself before He raised the dead.
blocks.es_reference: Las lágrimas de la muerte. María llora. Marta llora. Los plañideros profesionales lloran. Los vecinos judíos lloran. Y Jesús llora. Hace muchos años me senté con una mujer cuyo esposo la había dejado por otra mujer. Estaba reprimiendo su dolor, negándose a dejar que fuera real. El día que finalmente se permitió llorar fue el día en que comenzó a sanar. Las lágrimas son parte de cómo Dios suelta el corazón. El Señor no negó las lágrimas en Betania. Las derramó Él mismo antes de levantar al muerto.

blocks.en: The triumph of death. Jesus calls in a loud voice. Lazarus comes out. The graveclothes are still on him. Jesus says, Loose him, and let him go. The miracle does what the sentence said: I am the resurrection and the life. It is the sermon, preached with a tomb as the pulpit and a corpse as the demonstration. A pastor who reads this story only as a wonder misses what Jesus was teaching. He was not advertising His power. He was preaching Himself. The miracle is the message.
blocks.es_reference: El triunfo de la muerte. Jesús llama a gran voz. Lázaro sale. Los lienzos sepulcrales aún están sobre él. Jesús dice: desatadlo, y dejadle ir. El milagro hace lo que la oración dijo: Yo soy la resurrección y la vida. Es el sermón, predicado con una tumba como púlpito y un cadáver como demostración. Un pastor que lee esta historia solo como una maravilla pierde lo que Jesús estaba enseñando. No estaba haciendo publicidad de Su poder. Se estaba predicando a Sí mismo. El milagro es el mensaje.

blocks.en: 4. The Paralytic at Capernaum
blocks.es_reference: 4. El paralítico en Capernaum

blocks.en: If Lazarus shows the principle in its grandest form, Mark 2 shows it most plainly. Four friends bring a paralyzed man to Jesus by lowering him through the roof. The crowd is so thick they cannot reach Him any other way. Jesus looks at the paralytic and says something startling. He does not say, Rise and walk. He says, Son, your sins are forgiven you.
blocks.es_reference: Si Lázaro muestra el principio en su forma más grandiosa, Marcos 2 lo muestra más claramente. Cuatro amigos llevan a un hombre paralítico a Jesús bajándolo por el techo. La multitud es tan densa que no pueden alcanzarlo de otra manera. Jesús mira al paralítico y dice algo sorprendente. No dice: levántate y anda. Dice: hijo, tus pecados te son perdonados.

blocks.en: The scribes object silently. Only God can forgive sins. Jesus reads their thoughts and asks them a question that unlocks the whole gospel.
blocks.es_reference: Los escribas objetan en silencio. Solo Dios puede perdonar pecados. Jesús lee sus pensamientos y les hace una pregunta que abre todo el evangelio.

blocks.en: “Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Arise, take up your bed and walk’? But that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins... I say to you, arise, take up your bed, and go to your house.” (Mark 2:9–11, NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: «¿Qué es más fácil, decir al paralítico: Tus pecados te son perdonados, o decirle: Levántate, toma tu lecho y anda? Pues para que sepáis que el Hijo del Hombre tiene potestad en la tierra de perdonar pecados... a ti te digo: Levántate, toma tu lecho, y vete a tu casa.» (Marcos 2:9–11, RVG)

blocks.en: Read those verses slowly. Jesus tells us in plain language what every miracle of His is doing. That you may know. The miracle is performed so the invisible reality — forgiveness — can be seen. The paralytic stands up to prove the sins are gone. The visible act preaches the invisible truth. Mark’s entire Gospel is built on this rhythm. Christ heals so people will know who can forgive. Christ stills the storm so the disciples will ask, Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him? Christ feeds five thousand so the crowd will hear Him say, I am the bread of life. Every miracle preaches. Every miracle is an enacted parable.
blocks.es_reference: Lea esos versículos despacio. Jesús nos dice en lenguaje claro lo que cada milagro Suyo está haciendo. Para que sepáis. El milagro se realiza para que la realidad invisible — el perdón — pueda verse. El paralítico se levanta para probar que los pecados se han ido. El acto visible predica la verdad invisible. El Evangelio entero de Marcos está edificado sobre este ritmo. Cristo sana para que la gente sepa quién puede perdonar. Cristo calma la tormenta para que los discípulos pregunten: ¿quién es éste, que aun el viento y el mar le obedecen? Cristo alimenta a cinco mil para que la multitud Le oiga decir: Yo soy el pan de vida. Cada milagro predica. Cada milagro es una parábola representada.

blocks.en: 5. How to Read a Miracle Story
blocks.es_reference: 5. Cómo leer una historia de milagro

blocks.en: For every miracle you preach, ask four questions. First, what physical action does Jesus perform? A man is healed, a storm is stilled, water becomes wine. State the visible event plainly. Second, what does Jesus say before, during, or after the miracle? The spoken word almost always interprets the act. I am the resurrection. I am the bread of life. Your sins are forgiven. The spoken word is the key to the miracle. Third, what spiritual truth do the action and the word together preach? Resurrection from death. Provision in spiritual hunger. Forgiveness for sin. Authority over creation. Sight for the blind soul. Fourth, how does this truth meet the needs of the people who will hear my sermon? The visible miracle preached to the original eyewitnesses. The same truth preaches today to the same kinds of hearts.
blocks.es_reference: Para cada milagro que predique, haga cuatro preguntas. Primero, ¿qué acción física realiza Jesús? Un hombre es sanado, una tormenta se calma, el agua se convierte en vino. Declare el evento visible llanamente. Segundo, ¿qué dice Jesús antes, durante, o después del milagro? La palabra pronunciada casi siempre interpreta el acto. Yo soy la resurrección. Yo soy el pan de vida. Tus pecados te son perdonados. La palabra pronunciada es la llave del milagro. Tercero, ¿qué verdad espiritual predican juntos la acción y la palabra? Resurrección de la muerte. Provisión en el hambre espiritual. Perdón del pecado. Autoridad sobre la creación. Vista para el alma ciega. Cuarto, ¿cómo esta verdad responde a las necesidades de la gente que oirá mi sermón? El milagro visible predicó a los testigos oculares originales. La misma verdad predica hoy a las mismas clases de corazones.

blocks.en: Notice that none of the four questions is, How did Jesus do that scientifically? The miracle is not a physics problem. The miracle is a sermon in motion. The pastor whose Sunday morning is spent defending the chemistry of water becoming wine misses what John was teaching with that story.
blocks.es_reference: Note que ninguna de las cuatro preguntas es: ¿cómo hizo Jesús eso científicamente? El milagro no es un problema de física. El milagro es un sermón en movimiento. El pastor cuya mañana del domingo se gasta defendiendo la química del agua convertida en vino pierde lo que Juan estaba enseñando con esa historia.

blocks.en: 6. The Cardiologist in Chattanooga
blocks.es_reference: 6. El cardiólogo en Chattanooga

blocks.en: Dr. Maurice Rawlings was a heart specialist in Chattanooga, Tennessee. He was a nominal Christian when this happened. A patient came in for a treadmill stress test. The man had a heart attack during the test. Rawlings revived him. The patient was screaming, I feel the flames, do not let me go. He had another attack and the same thing happened. He had a third attack. Three times the man went to the edge.
blocks.es_reference: El Dr. Maurice Rawlings era un especialista del corazón en Chattanooga, Tennessee. Era cristiano nominal cuando esto sucedió. Un paciente vino para una prueba de esfuerzo en caminadora. El hombre tuvo un ataque al corazón durante la prueba. Rawlings lo reanimó. El paciente gritaba: siento las llamas, no me dejes ir. Tuvo otro ataque y sucedió lo mismo. Tuvo un tercer ataque. Tres veces el hombre fue al borde.

blocks.en: The third time, all Rawlings could remember was a verse he had learned in Sunday School: Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and thou shalt be saved. He asked the man, Do you believe? The man believed. The man lived. Rawlings re-examined his own faith, became active in his church, and the patient joined that church and served the Lord for the rest of his days.
blocks.es_reference: La tercera vez, todo lo que Rawlings podía recordar era un versículo que había aprendido en la Escuela Dominical: cree en el Señor Jesucristo, y serás salvo. Le preguntó al hombre: ¿crees? El hombre creyó. El hombre vivió. Rawlings volvió a examinar su propia fe, se volvió activo en su iglesia, y el paciente se unió a esa iglesia y sirvió al Señor por el resto de sus días.

blocks.en: That doctor was preaching the same sermon Jesus preached at the tomb of Lazarus. The patient’s revival was an enacted parable. The man came back from physical death three times so that he could be saved from spiritual death once. The body was the canvas; the soul was the painting. Read your own pastoral ministry that way and you will see God acting in your church the way He acted at Bethany. The healed body, the rescued marriage, the recovered addict, the answered prayer — every one of them is a sermon waiting for the pastor to interpret. Do not let the visible event remain unexplained. Speak the spoken word that turns the act into a sermon.
blocks.es_reference: Ese doctor estaba predicando el mismo sermón que Jesús predicó en la tumba de Lázaro. La reanimación del paciente fue una parábola representada. El hombre volvió de la muerte física tres veces para que pudiera ser salvado de la muerte espiritual una sola vez. El cuerpo era el lienzo; el alma era el cuadro. Lea su propio ministerio pastoral de esa manera y verá a Dios actuando en su iglesia de la manera en que actuó en Betania. El cuerpo sanado, el matrimonio rescatado, el adicto recuperado, la oración respondida — cada uno de ellos es un sermón esperando que el pastor lo interprete. No deje que el evento visible quede sin explicación. Pronuncie la palabra hablada que convierte el acto en sermón.

blocks.en: 7. Common Errors in Preaching Miracles
blocks.es_reference: 7. Errores comunes al predicar los milagros

blocks.en: Three errors trap many pastors when a miracle text comes up in the calendar. Each is a way of forgetting that the miracle is an enacted parable.
blocks.es_reference: Tres errores atrapan a muchos pastores cuando un texto de milagro aparece en el calendario. Cada uno es una manera de olvidar que el milagro es una parábola representada.

blocks.en: The naturalistic error. This is the modernist’s habit of explaining the miracle away. The feeding of the five thousand becomes a story about everyone sharing their hidden lunches. The stilling of the storm becomes Jesus catching a calm patch. The walking on water becomes a sandbar. The pastor who explains miracles away has nothing left to preach. The Author was not telling us a metaphor when He said Lazarus came out of the tomb. He was telling us a miracle. Let the miracle stand. Then preach it.
blocks.es_reference: El error naturalista. Éste es el hábito del modernista de explicar el milagro. La alimentación de los cinco mil se vuelve una historia sobre todos compartiendo sus loncheras ocultas. La calma de la tormenta se vuelve Jesús atrapando un parche calmo. El caminar sobre el agua se vuelve un banco de arena. El pastor que explica los milagros no tiene nada que predicar. El Autor no nos estaba contando una metáfora cuando dijo que Lázaro salió de la tumba. Nos estaba contando un milagro. Deje que el milagro permanezca. Luego predíquelo.

blocks.en: The spectacle error. The opposite mistake. The pastor stops at look how powerful Jesus is. He preaches a miracle as a thrill, but he never lets the miracle become a sermon. His congregation goes home impressed. They do not go home changed. The miracle was meant to preach the resurrection, the bread of life, the forgiveness of sin. Stop at the spectacle and you starve your people of the message.
blocks.es_reference: El error del espectáculo. El error opuesto. El pastor se detiene en miren qué poderoso es Jesús. Predica un milagro como una emoción, pero nunca deja que el milagro se vuelva un sermón. Su congregación se va a casa impresionada. No se va a casa cambiada. El milagro fue diseñado para predicar la resurrección, el pan de vida, el perdón del pecado. Deténgase en el espectáculo y matará de hambre a su pueblo privándolo del mensaje.

blocks.en: The allegorical error. Unit 6 warned us against this in parables. The same warning applies to miracles. We do not get to invent symbolic meanings for every detail. The five loaves are not the five books of Moses. The twelve baskets of leftovers are not the twelve apostles. Stay with the central word Jesus spoke alongside the miracle. That word is the authorized interpretation. Anything else is the preacher’s invention.
blocks.es_reference: El error alegórico. La Unidad 6 nos advirtió contra esto en las parábolas. La misma advertencia se aplica a los milagros. No podemos inventar significados simbólicos para cada detalle. Los cinco panes no son los cinco libros de Moisés. Los doce canastos de sobras no son los doce apóstoles. Quédese con la palabra central que Jesús pronunció junto al milagro. Esa palabra es la interpretación autorizada. Cualquier otra cosa es invención del predicador.

blocks.en: 8. Falling Asleep on the Couch
blocks.es_reference: 8. Quedarse dormido en el sofá

blocks.en: One evening a young boy who had been watching a program about death asked his mother, What is it like to die? She thought for a moment and said, It is like falling asleep on the couch in the evening, and waking up in your own bed. The reason is that your father picks you up and carries you off and tucks you in. In the same way, death for a Christian is like falling asleep — the Father comes and carries you off, and you wake up and find yourself in the right place.
blocks.es_reference: Una noche un niño que había estado viendo un programa sobre la muerte le preguntó a su mamá: ¿cómo es morir? Ella pensó un momento y dijo: es como quedarse dormido en el sofá por la noche, y despertar en tu propia cama. La razón es que tu papá te recoge y te lleva y te arropa. De la misma manera, la muerte para un cristiano es como quedarse dormido — el Padre viene y te recoge, y despiertas y te encuentras en el lugar correcto.

blocks.en: That mother was preaching the resurrection of Lazarus to her son in language his ears could carry. She was speaking the spoken word that interprets the visible reality of death. The miracle Jesus performed at Bethany was that same word made flesh — the Father, in His Son, picking up Lazarus and carrying him out of the tomb into the right place. A pastor who learns to read miracles as enacted parables can speak that same comfort in a thousand pastoral moments. A hospital room. A graveside. A widow at her kitchen table. The resurrection of Lazarus preaches there.
blocks.es_reference: Esa madre estaba predicando la resurrección de Lázaro a su hijo en un lenguaje que sus oídos podían cargar. Estaba pronunciando la palabra hablada que interpreta la realidad visible de la muerte. El milagro que Jesús realizó en Betania fue esa misma palabra hecha carne — el Padre, en Su Hijo, recogiendo a Lázaro y llevándolo fuera de la tumba al lugar correcto. Un pastor que aprende a leer los milagros como parábolas representadas puede pronunciar ese mismo consuelo en mil momentos pastorales. Una habitación de hospital. Junto a una tumba. Una viuda en la mesa de su cocina. La resurrección de Lázaro predica allí.

blocks.en: 9. The Pastor’s Sermon Method on a Miracle Text
blocks.es_reference: 9. El método sermónico del pastor en un texto de milagro

blocks.en: When a miracle text falls on your Sunday, work the four questions through in order. Find the visible action, find the spoken word, find the truth, find the application. Build your sermon to follow that pattern. Open with the visible event so your people see what Jesus did. Move to the spoken word so they hear what He said. Show how the two together preach a single truth about who Jesus is. Then bring that truth into the room where your people sit. I am the resurrection and the life meets the widow in the third row. Your sins are forgiven meets the addict trying to keep coming to church. I am the bread of life meets the businessman who has everything and is starving.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando un texto de milagro cae en su domingo, recorra las cuatro preguntas en orden. Encuentre la acción visible, encuentre la palabra pronunciada, encuentre la verdad, encuentre la aplicación. Construya su sermón para seguir ese patrón. Abra con el evento visible para que su pueblo vea lo que Jesús hizo. Pase a la palabra pronunciada para que oigan lo que Él dijo. Muestre cómo las dos juntas predican una sola verdad acerca de quién es Jesús. Luego lleve esa verdad al cuarto donde se sienta su pueblo. Yo soy la resurrección y la vida se encuentra con la viuda en la tercera fila. Tus pecados te son perdonados se encuentra con el adicto que sigue tratando de venir a la iglesia. Yo soy el pan de vida se encuentra con el empresario que tiene todo y se muere de hambre.

blocks.en: This pattern saves you from the three errors. It refuses to explain the miracle away, because the visible event is the first step. It refuses to stop at spectacle, because the spoken word is the second. It refuses to invent allegory, because the truth must be the one Jesus Himself named.
blocks.es_reference: Este patrón le salva de los tres errores. Se niega a explicar el milagro, porque el evento visible es el primer paso. Se niega a detenerse en el espectáculo, porque la palabra pronunciada es el segundo. Se niega a inventar alegoría, porque la verdad debe ser la que Jesús mismo nombró.

blocks.en: 10. Lazarus, Come Out
blocks.es_reference: 10. Lázaro, ven fuera

blocks.en: The last word in the Lazarus story is not Jesus’ word. It is the bystanders’. After Lazarus walks out of the cave still bound in his graveclothes, Jesus says, Loose him, and let him go. The miracle was Christ’s. The unbinding was His people’s. That is the picture of pastoral ministry. The Lord brings the dead back to life. We unwrap the graveclothes. Christ raises. The pastor releases.
blocks.es_reference: La última palabra en la historia de Lázaro no es la palabra de Jesús. Es la de los presentes. Después de que Lázaro sale de la cueva todavía atado en sus lienzos sepulcrales, Jesús dice: desatadlo, y dejadle ir. El milagro fue de Cristo. El desatar fue de Su pueblo. Ése es el cuadro del ministerio pastoral. El Señor trae al muerto de regreso a la vida. Nosotros desenvolvemos los lienzos sepulcrales. Cristo levanta. El pastor libera.

blocks.en: Pastor, every miracle in your Bible is preaching at you and through you. Listen to the spoken word that came alongside the act, and you will hear what Jesus wanted His people to know that they may believe. Preach the visible event as the visible sermon. Preach the spoken word as its interpretation. Then turn to your people, who are bound in their own graveclothes of sin and fear and grief, and say what the Lord told the Bethany crowd to say: Loose them, and let them go.
blocks.es_reference: Pastor, cada milagro en su Biblia le está predicando a usted y a través de usted. Escuche la palabra pronunciada que vino junto al acto, y oirá lo que Jesús quiso que Su pueblo supiera para que crean. Predique el evento visible como el sermón visible. Predique la palabra pronunciada como su interpretación. Luego vuélvase a su pueblo, que está atado en sus propios lienzos sepulcrales de pecado, temor, y duelo, y diga lo que el Señor le dijo a la multitud de Betania que dijera: desatadlos, y dejadlos ir.

mc.stem: The central thesis of this unit is that Christ's miracles are best understood as:
options: Random demonstrations of supernatural power
Enacted parables — visible actions that preach the same kind of truth a parable preaches
Advertising for Jesus' growing ministry
Tests of the disciples' faith levels
mc.why: Correct. A parable speaks truth in a story; a miracle speaks the same kind of truth in an action. The miracle is the visible word, and the spoken word interprets it. Both preach the same gospel.

mc.stem: The Greek word the Apostle John prefers for Jesus' miracles is:
options: Dynamis (power)
Teras (wonder)
Sêmeion (sign — something that points beyond itself)
Ergon (work)
mc.why: Correct. John calls Jesus' miracles SEMEIA — signs. A sign is not a destination; it is a pointer. The miracle directs attention to a spiritual reality the visible act is preaching.

mc.stem: The sentence Jesus speaks before raising Lazarus that interprets the entire miracle is:
options: "I am the resurrection and the life"
"Be still, my son"
"Father, glorify Your name"
"It is finished"
mc.why: Correct (John 11:25). Jesus speaks the sentence to Martha while Lazarus is still in the tomb. Minutes later He performs what He has just declared. Word and act together preach Christ's identity.

mc.stem: The four-part structure the lesson traces through the Lazarus story is:
options: Birth, life, death, resurrection
Tragedy, trial, tears, triumph
Sickness, decay, burial, mourning
Galilee, Judea, Bethany, Jerusalem
mc.why: Correct. The Tragedy (Lazarus dies), the Trial (Jesus delays on purpose), the Tears (Mary, Martha, mourners, and Jesus Himself weep), and the Triumph (Lazarus comes out). Each movement is part of one sermon Jesus is preaching with His hands and voice together.

mc.stem: In Mark 2, Jesus first tells the paralytic, "Your sins are forgiven you," and then heals him. The lesson reads this as:
options: A demonstration that physical healing is more important than forgiveness
An indication that Jesus did not know which problem to address first
The textbook miracle-as-enacted-parable: the visible healing preaches the invisible forgiveness
A coincidence that has nothing to do with the principle of enacted parables
mc.why: Correct. Jesus tells us explicitly in Mark 2:10 — "that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" — He performs the visible healing so the invisible forgiveness can be seen. This is the textbook miracle-as-enacted-parable.

mc.stem: According to Mark 2:10, Jesus heals the paralytic specifically:
options: To attract more disciples
Because the four friends had earned the favor
"That you may know the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins"
To prove He was a better physician than the local healers
mc.why: Correct. Mark 2:10 is one of the clearest examples in the NT of a miracle interpreting itself. The healing is performed so that the watching eyes can know what only God can do — forgive sin. The visible act preaches the invisible truth.

mc.stem: The lesson gives four questions a pastor should ask when preparing to preach a miracle. The first question is:
options: How can I scientifically explain what Jesus did?
Which Greek manuscript should I prefer?
What physical action does Jesus perform?
How long was the miracle remembered?
mc.why: Correct. Begin with the visible event. State it plainly: a man healed, a storm stilled, water turned to wine. The visible act is the canvas. Without naming the act, the rest of the sermon has nothing to rest on.

mc.stem: The second question the pastor should ask when preaching a miracle is:
options: What spoken word of Jesus interprets the miracle?
How can I make the miracle relatable to modern science?
What political event was happening that week?
What time of day did the miracle occur?
mc.why: Correct. The spoken word is the key to the miracle. "I am the resurrection." "I am the bread of life." "Your sins are forgiven." Find the sentence Jesus spoke alongside the miracle, and you have found the authorized interpretation of the act.

mc.stem: The Maurice Rawlings story (the cardiologist in Chattanooga whose patient had three heart attacks during one test) illustrates:
options: The danger of treadmill stress tests
The need for better hospital protocols
The skill of Tennessee cardiologists
A modern enacted parable — physical revival used to bring about spiritual rescue
mc.why: Correct. The patient came back from physical death three times so that he could be saved from spiritual death once. The body was the canvas; the soul was the painting. That is the same logic as Jesus' miracles — the visible event preaches the invisible truth.

mc.stem: The lesson identifies three common errors pastors make when preaching miracles. The first error is:
options: The naturalistic error — explaining the miracle away (e.g. five thousand were really just sharing hidden lunches)
Preaching the miracle on Sunday
Reading the text in Greek
Showing the congregation a map
mc.why: Correct. The modernist's habit is to explain miracles away — the feeding becomes sharing, the storm becomes a calm patch, the walking on water becomes a sandbar. The pastor who explains miracles away has nothing left to preach. Let the miracle stand.

mc.stem: The second common error this lesson warns against is:
options: The spectacle error — stopping at "look how powerful Jesus is" and never letting the miracle become a sermon
The geographic error
The chronological error
The translation error
mc.why: Correct. Preaching a miracle as a thrill leaves the congregation impressed but unchanged. The miracle was meant to PREACH a truth — resurrection, bread of life, forgiveness. Stop at the spectacle and you starve your people of the message.

mc.stem: The third common error this lesson warns against is:
options: Using a study Bible
The allegorical error — inventing symbolic meanings for every detail (e.g. five loaves = five books of Moses)
Preaching too quietly
Skipping the introduction
mc.why: Correct. Unit 6 warned us against this in parables, and the same warning applies to miracles. We do not get to invent symbols. Stay with the central word Jesus spoke alongside the miracle — that word is the authorized interpretation.

mc.stem: The lesson uses the "falling asleep on the couch" illustration to teach:
options: Children should not stay up late
Couches are better than beds for sleeping
Death for a Christian is the Father picking us up and carrying us to the right place — the same truth the Lazarus miracle preaches
Parents should not carry tired children
mc.why: Correct. The mother's words to her son speak the same truth Jesus enacted at Bethany. The Father, in His Son, picks up the dead and carries them into the right place. That is the resurrection preached in language a child can carry.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, the verse "Jesus wept" (John 11:35) teaches:
options: Jesus was overcome with His own grief and unable to act
Tears are a sign of spiritual weakness
Jesus did not yet know how the story would end
The Lord did not pretend death was nothing — He wept at it
mc.why: Correct. Death is a tragedy in the Bible — Jesus did not deny it. He wept at the tomb before He raised the dead. The shortest verse in the Bible is also one of the fullest: it teaches the pastor that grief is honored even when victory is coming.

mc.stem: The lesson says the pastor's role at the end of the Lazarus story is pictured by Jesus' command:
options: "Lazarus, come out"
"Take away the stone"
"Father, glorify Your name"
"Loose him, and let him go"
mc.why: Correct. The miracle was Christ's. The unbinding was His people's. "Loose him, and let him go" is the picture of pastoral ministry: the Lord raises the dead; the pastor unwraps the graveclothes. Christ raises; the pastor releases.

mc.stem: The lesson says feeding the five thousand was not really about the bread because:
options: The next day Jesus declared aloud "I am the bread of life" — the bread was the enacted parable of that spoken word
The bread was not very tasty
The crowd did not actually eat
There were not really five thousand people
mc.why: Correct. The miracle preached the next day's sermon in advance. The fish, the bread, the leftovers were not the point. Jesus is the bread. The miracle was the visible word; "I am the bread of life" was the spoken word that interpreted it.

mc.stem: The lesson teaches that the pastor's sermon method on a miracle text should:
options: Open with theology, then move to the text
Open with the visible event, move to the spoken word, then to the truth, then to the application
Open with personal experience, then defend the miracle scientifically
Open with the application and never return to the text
mc.why: Correct. The four-step pattern mirrors how Jesus Himself preached the miracle. Show what He did. Quote what He said. Connect the two as a single truth. Then carry that truth into the room where your people sit. The pattern protects you from the three errors.

mc.stem: The lesson teaches that Jesus' delay in coming to Lazarus (staying two more days after hearing of the sickness) was:
options: A failure of pastoral responsiveness
The canvas on which the miracle would be painted — the delay was part of how God prepared His people to see His glory
Evidence that He did not really love the family
A scheduling conflict with another teaching engagement
mc.why: Correct. The miracle would not have been a miracle if Jesus had arrived in time to prevent the death. The delay was the canvas. God's timing is not our timing, and delay is often how He prepares His people to see His glory.

mc.stem: The lesson's warning against the naturalistic error specifically rejects which kind of interpretation?
options: Reading the miracle as the visible act it actually was
Believing the spoken word that interprets the act
Applying the truth pastorally
"The crowd really just shared their hidden lunches" — or similar attempts to explain miracles away as ordinary events
mc.why: Correct. The naturalistic reading drains the miracle of its preaching power. The pastor who explains miracles away has nothing left to preach. Let the miracle stand as the text describes it; THEN preach what it preaches.

mc.stem: The closing charge of this unit to the pastor is:
options: Avoid miracles in preaching
Preach miracles only at Easter
Memorize each miracle in Greek
Preach the visible event as the visible sermon, the spoken word as its interpretation, and then say to your people, "Loose them, and let them go"
mc.why: Correct. The pastor's role is the unbinding — releasing the people Christ has raised from their own graveclothes of sin, fear, and grief. The Lord does the raising; the pastor does the releasing. That is the closing image of the unit.

fill.prompt: "I am the resurrection and the ____. He who believes in Me, though he may die, he shall live." (John 11:25)
John's preferred Greek word for Jesus' miracles, sêmeion, means ____: something that points beyond itself.
The point of the feeding of the five thousand was the ____ of Life, which Jesus declared aloud the next day in John 6.
Jesus stayed where He was two more days before going to Bethany; the ____ was the canvas on which the miracle would be painted.
When Jesus healed the paralytic lowered through the roof, the miracle was performed so that the invisible reality of ____ could be seen.
Because the spoken word almost always interprets the act, the spoken word is the ____ to the miracle.
The modernist habit of explaining miracles away, such as turning the walking on water into a sandbar, is called the ____ error.
The pastor who stops at "look how powerful Jesus is" and preaches a miracle as a thrill commits the ____ error.
With his patient at the edge of death, Dr. Rawlings remembered a Sunday School verse: "Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and thou shalt be ____."
After Lazarus came out still bound in his graveclothes, Jesus told the bystanders, "____ him, and let him go"; Christ raises, and the pastor releases.

sa.prompt: Tell the story of Lazarus (John 11) in your own words and explain why the lesson calls this miracle an "enacted parable."
sa.model: At Bethany, four days after Lazarus was buried, Jesus stood before the sealed tomb, wept, and called him out — having declared, 'I am the resurrection and the life.' The word and the act are one teaching: the miracle is not separate from the sermon. The raising of Lazarus is an enacted parable preaching that Jesus is the resurrection and the life.

sa.prompt: Define the Greek word sêmeion and explain why John's choice of this term for Jesus' miracles teaches the central principle of this unit.
sa.model: John chose the Greek word sêmeion, meaning 'sign,' for Jesus' miracles rather than a word for raw wonder. A sign is not the destination; it points beyond itself to a truth. By calling the miracles signs, John teaches the central principle of the unit: every miracle points beyond the visible event to an invisible truth about Christ.

sa.prompt: Trace the four-T structure of the Lazarus story (Tragedy, Trial, Tears, Triumph) and explain what each movement contributes to the enacted parable.
sa.model: The Lazarus story moves through four movements. Tragedy: Lazarus sickens and dies. Trial: Jesus delays on purpose, and the sisters wait in grief. Tears: Jesus weeps at the tomb. Triumph: He calls Lazarus out alive. Each movement is part of one sermon, turning death and delay into the glory of God.

sa.prompt: Explain how Mark 2:9-11 (the paralytic at Capernaum) is the clearest textbook example of a miracle being performed to preach an invisible truth.
sa.model: In Mark 2, when four friends lowered a paralytic to Jesus, He first said, 'Your sins are forgiven.' Then, 'that you may know the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins,' He healed the man. The visible healing was performed to preach the invisible truth that Jesus has authority to forgive. It is the clearest textbook case of a miracle enacting a sermon.

sa.prompt: List the four questions the lesson recommends a pastor ask before preaching any miracle text, and briefly explain each.
sa.model: Before preaching any miracle text the pastor asks four questions: What is the visible action Jesus performed? What is the spoken word that interprets it? What invisible truth does the sign preach? And what is the application — the need in my people that this truth meets? The questions move from the visible act to the truth to the listener's need.

sa.prompt: Tell the Maurice Rawlings story (the Chattanooga cardiologist and the patient with three heart attacks) and explain how it functions as a modern enacted parable.
sa.model: Dr. Maurice Rawlings, a Chattanooga cardiologist, was a nominal Christian when a patient had repeated heart attacks during a stress test, screaming in terror between revivals. Rawlings led him to Christ with a verse from Sunday School. The man came back from physical death so he could be saved from spiritual death once — an enacted parable, the body the canvas and the soul the painting.

sa.prompt: Name and briefly describe the three common errors pastors make when preaching miracle texts.
sa.model: Three errors plague the preaching of miracle texts. The naturalistic error explains the miracle away as something ordinary. The spectacle error stops at the thrill of the wonder without the truth it preaches. The allegorical error invents a meaning for every detail Jesus left alone. Each error keeps the sign from pointing where Jesus aimed it.

sa.prompt: Explain why the lesson rejects the naturalistic explanation of miracles (e.g. "the crowd really just shared their hidden lunches"), and what is lost when a pastor adopts that reading.
sa.model: The lesson rejects the naturalistic reading — that the feeding of the five thousand was really just the crowd sharing hidden lunches. To explain the miracle away is the modernist move, and it leaves nothing to preach: a Christ who only inspired sharing has no power to save. When the miracle is explained away, the gospel power in it is lost.

sa.prompt: Tell the "falling asleep on the couch" illustration and explain how it connects to the resurrection of Lazarus.
sa.model: A child who falls asleep on the couch is carried by his father to his own bed and wakes there in the morning. That is a picture of death for the Christian: we fall asleep here and the Father carries us, waking in His house. It connects to Lazarus, of whom Jesus said, 'Our friend sleeps' — for the believer death is only a sleep from which Christ raises us.

sa.prompt: Explain the closing image of the unit: Jesus' command "Loose him, and let him go" as a picture of pastoral ministry.
sa.model: After raising Lazarus, Jesus told the bystanders, 'Loose him, and let him go.' Christ raises the dead to life; then He hands the work of unbinding the graveclothes to others. That is a picture of pastoral ministry: Christ gives new life, and the pastor's task is to loose and release those He has raised, freeing them from what still binds them.
